text:
Interviewer: The following is an interview with Pete Miller. The interview is being conducted at the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum, on October 7th, 1993, by Jack Smith. Please tell us your full name.
Interviewee: Pete Miller.
Interviewer: And when were you born and where were you born?
Interviewee: December 7, 1915, Kielce, Poland.
Interviewer: Could you describe your household growing up, who — who you lived with?
Interviewee: Mm-hm. My parents, two —
Interviewer: And their names?
Interviewee: Hans and Floor Miller. Mother’s maiden name was Cox, c-o-x. Two sisters, two older sisters. The oldest was Alice, the younger was Olivia, and myself and my younger brother, whose name was very hard, *** this was six of us.
Interviewer: What kind of work did your father do?
Interviewee: He was a businessman. He was representing for a quite long time, a factory manufacturing pots and pans and selling. And then lately, just before the war, he was owning his property which was not far away from Kielce, by the name of Ludinya, not far away from Czestochowa. They were digging out their *** which was going on the beginning for cleaning sugar, later to dig out which was going for china. War came and everything fell apart.
Interviewer: Did you live right in the main part of the city, did you live in the outskirts?
Interviewee: No, we live i-in town of Kielce, in the city.
Interviewer: Right in the city.
Interviewee: That’s right.
Interviewer: What kind of neighborhood was it?
Interviewee: Very hard to describe what kind.
Interviewer: Mix?
Interviewee: A mix what is —
Interviewer: Jews and non-Jews?
Interviewee: Kielce — Kielce was — I don’t think that had more than 10 percent of Jewish population, and — but this was a mix one neighborhood, I would say, 10 percent maybe Jewish and 90 percent not Jewish. I was there til 1932, and 1932 I left for Warsaw.
Interviewer: What kind of schooling did you have?
Interviewee: I — in Kielce I graduated gymnasium, and then four years of law school in Warsaw. In 1939 the war started, and this was the end.
Interviewer: Did your — was your family a religious family?
Interviewee: Let’s say this way, my father was a believer in religious sense. They were not like are here, you know, Reform, Conservative, and — no, didn’t have a beard, if you understand this. On Friday when he made prayers, he took off the hat and that’s what it was.
Interviewer: Did you have any kind of religious training yourself?
Interviewee: Yeah, I know still how to read Hebrew.
Interviewer: And how did you learn that?
Interviewee: Teacher was coming home and teaching us, only me and my brother.
Interviewer: And when you went to school, you went to school with non-Jewish children?
Interviewee: When I started to school, I was the only one Jewish fellow. When I was ending the school was probably something around 15. Together, the whole school had around 500 pupils.
Interviewer: Do — do you —
Interviewee: This was a state school.
Interviewer: Do you recall any anti-Semitic incidents growing up? Any problems because you were Jewish, as a child?
Interviewee: Not to the point that I experienced later.
Interviewer: Right, but anything growing up? Did you —
Interviewee: From time to time remarks. I was very good in sport, so I was getting much less that probably did get, all boys who were going to Jewish schools.
Interviewer: What kind of sports did you do?
Interviewee: Soccer was the first and tennis second.
Interviewer: So you were on teams with non-Jewish —
Interviewee: Yeah.
Interviewer: All right. And then you stayed in Kielce — Kielce for how long?
Interviewee: Til 1932.
Interviewer: 1932, and you were 17 by that time?
Interviewee: That’s correct.
Interviewer: And where did you go?
Interviewee: To Warsaw.
Interviewer: To do what?
Interviewee: To university of Warsaw, to study, and in 1936, I finish, and I had only three years of optic — of m —
Interviewer: Apprenticeship.
Interviewer: — apprenticeship in — as a lawyer, and the war started and this was an end of my profession.
Interviewer: All right. And living in Warsaw from 1932, before the war, what was that like? Can you describe —
Interviewee: I was a student and I already distan — decided not to take any more money from my father, so I was working already in the lawyer’s office and making money helping the lawyer, being already — you know, you didn’t have to go every day to the law school, you needed to take only exams on the end of the year, school year. So I had enough time to go and to do this, and I was doing — being honest, I wa — didn’t like too much the law, I — I preferred to be probably just an engineer, but this was not the profession which you could do in Poland, especially for a Jewish fellow. And in family of four we were five lawyers. My brother-in-law, the oldest one was a lawyer. My oldest sister was a lawyer, my youngest sister was a lawyer.
Interviewer: And so you — when you went to Warsaw, were you living by yourself?
Interviewee: Yeah, I was living on ***
Interviewer: O-On a what?
Interviewee: ***
Interviewer: Yes, uh-huh, uh-huh. And any problems in 1932 - ’33 - ’34 with —
Interviewee: Anti-Semitic?
Interviewer: Yeah.
Interviewee: Yes, on the university —
Interviewer: And do you —
Interviewee: — but as I said before, we did not go every day.
Interviewer: Right.
Interviewee: So —
Interviewer: Which university were you a student at?
Interviewee: Warsaw was the university, which had name later Pilsudski, but in my time was Warsaw University, and —
Interviewer: Can you describe one of the incidents early on in Warsaw?
Interviewee: Yes, yes, I do, because one of my friends from Kielce, which we were in school together, was also studying law. We went one day, was purpose, because you know, they told to sit on the left side, and he did sit down also.
Interviewer: They told who to sit on the left side?
Interviewee: The professor said the Jewish people stood and should sit on the left side. And when we’re going out, they were waiting for us, you know, and was purpose, to show that we are not afraid, I showed him to go out first, and he knew what’s going on, so he showed me, and I went, so he got beaten up.
Interviewer: By other students?
Interviewee: That’s right. And I knew about others, I didn’t experience too much myself, because as I said, I was going there only for on the end of the year to take the exams, and that’s all what was.
Interviewer: Mm-hm, mm-hm, mm-hm. All right. And then the years — it was 1935 - ’36?
Interviewee: Th-Th — ’36.
Interviewer: And you finished law s —
Interviewee: School in 1936.
Interviewer: And then what did you do?
Interviewee: That’s a — what I said I pul — went to the lawyer for a — usually you could go to that court for three years and then to have two years with the lawyer or you could go for five years with the lawyer. And so I decided to take this five years and after three years was already everything over, so I didn’t graduate, you know, I didn’t pass the bar exams because I wasn’t — didn’t have the five years.
Interviewer: Right, right. And then —
Interviewee: And the rest is history.
Interviewer: And the rest is history. Lo — okay, let’s talk about now with the war breaking out, because up to that point you were doing your re — working with the court.
Interviewee: Right.
Interviewer: Okay. And then when your — your first memories of when the war started, can you describe —
Interviewee: That first memory?
Interviewer: Yeah, of when the war started.
Interviewee: In 1939, as a matter of fact we were on vacation. When I say we were — because it happens that my wife was there on vacation too, together.
Interviewer: Were you married at that time?
Interviewee: No.
Interviewer: Oh, okay.
Interviewee: We met only in 1935, this was the year my wife graduate from high school in Warsaw. But in 1939 we found ourselves in the same hotel in the country on vacation. And as a matter of fact —
